title: Finding work does not ensure a secure livelihood
source: Source: 2025 Multi-Country Survey on Socio-Economic Vulnerabilities of Roma. Quotes from the micro-narratives study.

sections.title: For young Roma, the move from learning into work offers few secure routes forward

content.content: Half of Roma aged 16 to 24 are outside employment, education and training, compared with around one in six nearby non-Roma. The gap is particularly wide for young women. These figures cover people with different circumstances, including responsibilities at home and efforts to find a course or a job.

content.title: Young people not in employment, education or training (NEET)
content.subTitle: Share of all people aged 16 to 24 who are neither employed nor in education or training, shown for Roma and nearby non-Roma, overall and by sex

content.content: One young Roma woman describes applying for training and being turned away. Her account shows how an opportunity can be available locally yet remain out of reach:

“I want to have access to training but it is not fair… there were some courses but Roma women did not take the training but only non-Roma, I applied but they did not select me… many Roma women cannot compete with the formal training of non-Roma women.”
content.author: Female, aged 18 to 23

microViz.text: young Roma women are not in employment, education or training

sections.title: Steady work with sufficient income and protection remains out of reach for many Roma

content.content: Women have fewer openings into paid work; men more often work without formal protection. Roma women are about half as likely as Roma men to be employed, and both are less likely to have work than their non-Roma neighbours. Men’s higher employment also comes with greater informality.
For many, earning an income means working without the contracts or social contributions that provide protection beyond the next payment.

content.content: Families piece together a living through seasonal labour, trading and occasional jobs. People combine activities and arrange working hours around family responsibilities. But earnings can stop while rent, food and utility expenses continue.

“No matter how much I work… it’s still not enough to live on… my salary goes to rent, utilities, and especially food. Everything has become very expensive now, and we don’t even have enough for food.”
content.author: Female, aged 30 to 49

sections.title: An unexpected expense is beyond most households’ means

content.content: Most Roma live in households unable to cover an unexpected required expense. Nearby non-Roma households also face this pressure, though less often and less intensely. For families already struggling with regular bills, one extra cost can mean falling further behind on payments.
